analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from making job decisions by algorithm alone and gives workers a human appeal.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2024, referred to three House committees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The No Robot Bosses Act would stop employers with 11 or more workers from letting software alone hire, fire, discipline, pay, or schedule people. Any algorithm used in a job decision would have to be tested for bias each year, explained to the worker in plain language, and backed up by a human reviewer, with the worker able to dispute the result and appeal to a different human. Workers could also opt out of being managed by an algorithm and get a human manager instead. The bill would create a new Technology and Worker Protection Division in the Labor Department to enforce these rules, let workers and unions sue with statutory damages of up to $40,000 per violation, and make it illegal to retaliate against workers who complain.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at employers of 11 or more people. Anyone screened out by an automated hiring tool, denied a raise or hours by a scheduling algorithm, or disciplined based on software scores would get advance notice, a plain-language explanation, testing of the system for bias, a human double-check, and a way to dispute and appeal. Workers managed by algorithms could opt out and get a human manager. Workers and unions could sue, with damages of $5,000 to $40,000 per violation plus attorney's fees, and could not be forced into pre-dispute arbitration or barred from class actions for these claims [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Employers could not rely exclusively on an automated decision system for any hiring, firing, discipline, pay, scheduling, or promotion decision; a human with relevant experience would have to independently corroborate the algorithm's output [S2].

Before using an algorithm in a job decision, the employer would have to test it for discriminatory impact against race, sex, age, disability, pregnancy, and other protected traits, and re-test it annually with results made public [S2].

Workers would get advance notice that an algorithm is being used, a plain-language explanation of what data feeds it and how it scores them, free documentation within 7 days of any decision, and the right to dispute the output and appeal to a different human [S2].
Workers managed through an automated system could opt out and be managed by a human manager instead [S2].

The bill creates a Technology and Worker Protection Division inside the Labor Department to investigate employers, gives workers and unions a private right to sue with statutory damages of $5,000-$40,000 per violation ($10,000-$40,000+ for willful or repeat violations) and attorney's fees, lets state attorneys general enforce, and voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims [S2].
Employers could not fire, demote, threaten, or otherwise retaliate against a worker for complaining about or exercising rights under the act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more workers that use automated hiring, evaluation, scheduling, or management tools, and the vendors that sell those systems. They would bear testing and annual bias-audit costs, new disclosure paperwork, human oversight on every algorithm-assisted decision, appeal processes, litigation exposure with statutory damages, and lost ability to force such disputes into individual arbitration. Federal and state labor and consumer-protection agencies would bear the cost of standing up a new enforcement division and advisory boards [S2].

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is heavy even for mid-sized employers: annual third-party bias testing, detailed pre-use disclosures, free documentation to every affected worker within 7 days of each decision, training for system operators, and human corroboration of every algorithm-assisted decision. The text does not provide dedicated funding for the new Labor Department division, so its cost would fall on appropriations [S2].

The definition of an automated decision system is broad, covering any software that aids or informs employment decisions, which could sweep in ordinary HR tools like spreadsheet-based scheduling or keyword resume filters and generate litigation over what counts [S2].

Statutory damages of $5,000-$40,000 per covered individual, plus a private right of action and attorney's fees, give plaintiffs' lawyers a strong incentive to sue over paperwork violations even where no worker was actually harmed by the algorithm's substance [S2].

Requiring a human to corroborate and allowing workers to opt out of algorithmic management does not by itself guarantee human managers are better; it can slow decisions and shift costs to smaller employers near the 11-worker threshold [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a real and growing problem: automated tools already screen out job applicants and set workers' schedules and pay with little transparency or recourse. The bill's core requirement — no purely algorithmic job decisions, tested for bias, explained, and appealable to a human — is a straightforward safeguard. The costs are real but conventional for new workplace regulation, and the 11-employee threshold spares the smallest businesses. The main design risk is litigation exposure from statutory damages and a very broad definition of covered software, which opponents could have narrowed in committee. As introduced, the benefits to workers outweigh the compliance costs, though a negotiated version would likely have softened the damages provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, none of which acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the No Robot Bosses Act on March 12, 2024, joined by Rep. Chris Deluzio as its only cosponsor [S1][S2][S3].
The same day, the bill was referred to the Education and Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight committees; no further action was ever taken [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred in either chamber, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use automated hiring and management tools, and the vendors that sell them, are better off: they face none of the testing, disclosure, human-oversight, and litigation obligations the bill would have imposed. Workers who deal with algorithmic management got no new federal protections from this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two House Democrats behind it and no Republican cosponsors; with a Republican House majority and committee control, it never advanced past referral, making the partisan shape lopsided though never tested by a vote.

industries.industry: HR technology and AI hiring-software vendors
industries.note: The bill would require pre-deployment testing, annual independent bias audits with public results, and disclosure of the vendor's identity to every worker whose data feeds the system, alongside liability that follows the employer. Vendors profit from selling opaque scoring systems into workplaces; the bill makes transparency and testing the price of that market [S2].

industries.industry: Large employers using automated hiring, scheduling, and management tools
industries.note: Employers would face testing, disclosure, human-oversight, and appeal obligations and statutory-damages exposure, but the bill does not ban the tools; employers that can absorb the compliance costs keep algorithmic systems as a permanent part of running their workforce, now with a federal framework that legitimizes their use [S2].

The private right of action, statutory damages of $5,000-$40,000 per violation, mandatory attorney's fees, and a ban on pre-dispute arbitration and class-action waivers would open a large new litigation avenue for representing workers [S2].
